difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain in a medical context. The gap between 'approved for clinical use' and 'safe for patients' requires a bridging universal. One trap reverses the conditional; another weakens with 'generally.'
stimulus: A new analgesic compound has completed all three phases of clinical trials without producing serious adverse events in any participant. The regulatory agency has therefore approved it for clinical use. Dr. Reyes concludes that the compound is safe for patients to use.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any compound approved for clinical use by the regulatory agency is safe for patients to use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any compound safe for patients to use will be approved for clinical use by the regulatory agency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most compounds that complete all three phases of clinical trials without serious adverse events are safe for patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No compound that produces serious adverse events in clinical trials should ever be approved for clinical use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Compounds that are safe for patients to use rarely produce serious adverse events during clinical trials.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'approved for clinical use' to 'safe for patients.' The only link that forces the conclusion is a universal conditional: approved → safe. Choice A supplies exactly this link, making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.B: This reverses the required conditional (safe → approved), leaving the gap between approval and safety unbridged.
explanations.C: 'Most' is too weak — it allows for exceptions and does not guarantee this compound is safe.
explanations.D: This concerns compounds that should not be approved, which is irrelevant to whether an approved compound is safe.
explanations.E: This runs the conditional in the wrong direction and uses 'rarely,' a hedge that cannot force any conclusion.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in economics: the argument jumps from 'reduces consumer spending' to 'slows GDP growth.' Students must supply the conditional bridge. A trap answer conflates cause and effect direction.
stimulus: An economist argues that the recently enacted tariff on imported consumer electronics will reduce consumer spending on those goods. She therefore concludes that the tariff will slow overall GDP growth in the country.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tariffs on imported goods always produce trade deficits that reduce GDP growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any policy that reduces consumer spending on a significant category of goods will slow overall GDP growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overall GDP growth tends to slow whenever consumer confidence declines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slowing GDP growth in a country will generally reduce consumer spending on imported goods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most economists agree that tariffs on electronics are harmful to economic growth.

explanations.correct: The argument needs a bridge from 'reduces consumer spending on a significant goods category' to 'slows overall GDP growth.' Choice B is a universal conditional that closes this gap exactly, making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: Introduces trade deficits, a concept absent from the stimulus, and commits to a different causal mechanism than the one the economist uses.
explanations.C: 'Consumer confidence' is not mentioned in the stimulus; this is a partial bridge using a different concept.
explanations.D: This reverses the causal direction — slow GDP → reduced spending — rather than reduced spending → slow GDP.
explanations.E: 'Most economists agree' is an appeal to authority, not a conditional link, and cannot force the conclusion logically.

difficultyReason: Two-step gap in environmental science. The argument moves from 'increased surface runoff' to 'degraded water quality in the reservoir.' Students must bridge these via a universal conditional. Trap choices use hedges or shift the subject to groundwater.
stimulus: Deforestation along the Miren River watershed has substantially increased surface runoff into the river during rainfall events. Hydrologists therefore conclude that water quality in the downstream reservoir will degrade.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deforestation always reduces the biodiversity of the affected watershed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any substantial increase in surface runoff into a river will degrade water quality in any downstream reservoir fed by that river.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water quality in most reservoirs tends to decline when upstream land use changes occur.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Degraded water quality in a reservoir will typically increase surface runoff in the surrounding watershed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Groundwater quality in areas affected by deforestation is generally lower than in forested areas.

explanations.correct: The argument needs a universal bridge from 'substantial increase in surface runoff' to 'degraded reservoir water quality.' Choice B supplies exactly this conditional, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Biodiversity is irrelevant to the argument's conclusion about water quality.
explanations.C: 'Most reservoirs' and 'tends to decline' are too weak — they allow for exceptions and do not guarantee degradation in this case.
explanations.D: This reverses the causal direction: degraded quality → increased runoff, the opposite of what the argument requires.
explanations.E: Groundwater is a different subject from the surface runoff and reservoir water quality at issue in the argument.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in law. The argument moves from 'signed without legal counsel' to 'contract is unenforceable.' Students must supply the missing universal conditional. A reversed-conditional trap and a 'generally' hedge trap are present.
stimulus: When Denholm signed the licensing agreement, he had not yet retained legal counsel and did not fully understand the indemnification clause. His attorney now argues that the contract is unenforceable against Denholm.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any contract signed by a party who did not fully understand a material clause is unenforceable against that party.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any contract that is unenforceable against a party was signed without full understanding of its material clauses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contracts signed without legal counsel are generally considered unenforceable in most jurisdictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An indemnification clause is always the most important clause in a licensing agreement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No contract signed without legal counsel can be considered legally binding on either party.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that Denholm did not fully understand the indemnification clause (a material clause) and concludes the contract is unenforceable. Choice A supplies the universal conditional — not understanding a material clause → unenforceable — that makes the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.B: This reverses the conditional: unenforceable → signed without understanding. It does not bridge from Denholm's lack of understanding to unenforceability.
explanations.C: 'Generally considered' and 'most jurisdictions' are too weak and do not guarantee unenforceability in Denholm's case.
explanations.D: Importance of the clause is irrelevant; the argument turns on comprehension, not significance.
explanations.E: The argument focuses on Denholm's failure to understand the clause, not on the absence of counsel per se; E also over-extends to both parties.

difficultyReason: Two-step gap in technology/policy. The argument moves from 'collects data without user consent' to 'violates users' privacy rights.' The correct answer supplies the universal bridge. A trap introduces a scope shift to 'personal data'; another trap uses 'usually.'
stimulus: The fitness-tracking application automatically uploads users' location data to a third-party advertising network without obtaining explicit user consent. A consumer-rights group concludes that the application violates users' privacy rights.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any application that collects personal data without consent is likely to be used for commercial purposes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any application that transmits a user's data to a third party without the user's explicit consent violates that user's privacy rights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Users whose privacy rights are violated usually had their data transmitted without consent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Location data is the most sensitive category of personal data that an application can collect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Advertising networks that receive user data without consent often misuse that data.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that user data is transmitted to a third party without consent and concludes that privacy rights are violated. Choice B is the universal conditional — transmits data without consent → violates privacy rights — that forces the conclusion.
explanations.A: Commercial purpose is a different concept from privacy violation; this choice does not bridge to the conclusion.
explanations.C: This reverses the direction: violated rights → transmitted without consent. It does not force the conclusion from the given facts.
explanations.D: The relative sensitivity of location data is irrelevant; the argument turns on consent, not data type.
explanations.E: 'Often misuse' is too weak and concerns downstream harm rather than the violation of rights established by the transmission itself.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in linguistics. The argument moves from 'language lacks written records before 1500' to 'cannot be classified as a literary language.' Students must supply the universal conditional. A trap widens the scope incorrectly; another trap uses 'most.'
stimulus: Linguists have confirmed that Vashiri, a language spoken in the northern highlands, has no written records predating the sixteenth century. A historian therefore argues that Vashiri cannot be classified as a literary language in the premodern period.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most languages spoken in the northern highlands lack written records from the premodern period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A language can be classified as a literary language in a given period only if it has written records from that period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a language has written records from a period, it will always be classified as a literary language for that period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No language spoken in the northern highlands has ever been classified as a literary language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Languages that lack written records are generally less complex than those that have them.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Vashiri cannot be a literary language in the premodern period because it lacks written records from that time. Choice B supplies the necessary conditional: literary language classification requires written records from the period. With this premise, the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: 'Most languages' is too weak and discusses other languages, not the classification criterion for Vashiri.
explanations.C: This runs the conditional in the permissive direction (records → literary) rather than the restrictive direction (no records → not literary) required to force the conclusion.
explanations.D: This overstates the case by ruling out all highland languages, and does not rest on the written-records criterion used in the argument.
explanations.E: Complexity is a different dimension from literary classification; this choice does not bridge to the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in ethics/policy. The argument moves from 'receiving payment for endorsement without disclosure' to 'acting deceptively toward consumers.' Correct answer supplies the universal bridge. Trap reverses direction; another trap shifts subject to advertisers.
stimulus: A prominent nutrition blogger accepted payment from a supplement company to promote its products in posts but never disclosed this financial relationship to readers. An ethics board argues that the blogger acted deceptively toward consumers.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who acts deceptively toward consumers has accepted payment without making the required disclosures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Supplement companies that pay bloggers for promotion without requiring disclosure are themselves acting deceptively.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who accepts payment to endorse a product and fails to disclose that arrangement to the audience is acting deceptively toward that audience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deceptive endorsements usually involve financial relationships between content creators and the companies whose products they promote.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Readers of nutrition blogs generally assume that product endorsements are unpaid unless otherwise disclosed.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that the blogger accepted payment and failed to disclose it, then concludes the blogger acted deceptively. Choice C is a universal conditional — paid undisclosed endorsement → deceptive act toward audience — that makes the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: This reverses the required conditional: deceptive → undisclosed payment. It does not force the conclusion from the established facts.
explanations.B: The subject shifts to the supplement company, not the blogger whose conduct is under scrutiny.
explanations.D: 'Usually involve' is too weak; it does not guarantee that this blogger's conduct was deceptive.
explanations.E: Reader assumptions make the deception more plausible but do not logically force the conclusion that the blogger acted deceptively.

difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain in history. The argument moves from 'city lost its primary trade route' to 'city experienced economic decline.' Students must bridge these two concepts with a universal conditional. A trap introduces a temporal hedge; another trap shifts subject to regional economies.
stimulus: Historical records indicate that the port city of Calentum lost access to its primary Mediterranean trade route in the third century CE after a series of silting events blocked its harbor. Scholars argue that Calentum therefore experienced economic decline during this period.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any city that loses access to its primary trade route will experience economic decline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any city that experiences economic decline has previously lost access to an important trade route.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cities dependent on maritime trade routes often struggle economically when those routes are disrupted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silting events in the third century CE affected the economies of most Mediterranean port cities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economic decline in regional trade networks usually follows from the loss of multiple major ports simultaneously.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from loss of primary trade route to economic decline. Choice A is a universal conditional — loses primary trade route → economic decline — that bridges the gap and forces the conclusion.
explanations.B: This reverses the conditional: economic decline → prior loss of trade route. It does not force economic decline from the loss of the route.
explanations.C: 'Often struggle' is too weak; it permits exceptions and does not guarantee decline for Calentum.
explanations.D: Other Mediterranean cities are irrelevant; the argument is specifically about Calentum and its primary route.
explanations.E: The argument concerns a single city losing one route, not the simultaneous loss of multiple ports across a region.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in arts/criticism. The argument moves from 'the composer borrowed melodic material without attribution' to 'the symphony is not an original work.' Correct answer supplies universal bridge. Trap uses 'most'; another trap shifts subject to the publisher.
stimulus: Musicologists have established that the finale of Brandt's Fifth Symphony incorporates several melodic passages drawn directly from unpublished folk songs collected by a regional ethnographer, without any acknowledgment of this source. A critic concludes that the symphony cannot be considered an original work.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No work that incorporates unattributed material drawn from another source can be considered an original work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most symphonies that borrow from folk traditions are not considered original works by musicologists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any work that cannot be considered original was composed by borrowing melodic material from unattributed sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Publishers who release works containing unattributed borrowed material are responsible for the lack of attribution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Folk songs that were never published cannot be protected by intellectual property law.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that Brandt's symphony incorporates unattributed borrowed material and concludes it is not original. Choice A supplies the universal conditional — unattributed borrowed material → not original — making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.B: 'Most symphonies' and 'most musicologists' introduce a hedge and a scope shift; this cannot guarantee the conclusion about Brandt's specific symphony.
explanations.C: This reverses the conditional: not original → borrowed unattributed material. It does not force the originality conclusion from the established facts.
explanations.D: The publisher's responsibility is a different subject from whether the symphony itself is original.
explanations.E: Intellectual property law is irrelevant to the question of whether the work is original in the critical/artistic sense.

difficultyReason: Two-step gap in policy/public health. The argument moves from 'program reduces sedentary behavior' to 'program will reduce rates of type 2 diabetes.' Students must bridge these two concepts. Trap reverses direction; another trap uses 'tends to.'
stimulus: A public health agency has introduced a community exercise program that has been shown to significantly reduce sedentary behavior among participants. The agency concludes that the program will reduce rates of type 2 diabetes in the community.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any intervention that reduces rates of type 2 diabetes must first reduce sedentary behavior among the target population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any program that significantly reduces sedentary behavior in a community will reduce rates of type 2 diabetes in that community.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sedentary behavior tends to increase the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes in most populations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Community exercise programs are the most cost-effective means of addressing type 2 diabetes rates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rates of type 2 diabetes in a community are determined primarily by the level of physical activity among residents.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that the program reduces sedentary behavior and concludes it will reduce type 2 diabetes rates. Choice B supplies the universal conditional — significantly reduces sedentary behavior → reduces type 2 diabetes rates — that closes the gap and forces the conclusion.
explanations.A: This reverses the conditional: reduces diabetes → must reduce sedentary behavior. It does not force the diabetes reduction conclusion from the established reduction in sedentary behavior.
explanations.C: 'Tends to increase' and 'most populations' are too weak; they do not guarantee this program's effect on diabetes rates in this community.
explanations.D: Cost-effectiveness is irrelevant to whether the program will actually reduce diabetes rates.
explanations.E: 'Determined primarily by' does not establish a sufficient conditional relationship; other factors could override physical activity, so the conclusion does not follow necessarily.
